direct_claims: This chart reports how young people in selected countries responded “yes” to several statements about climate change in 2021.
The subject is youth opinion on climate-related threat perceptions.
The chart states that 1,000 young people aged 16 to 25 were surveyed in each country.
It also includes an “All countries” summary alongside individual countries.
The source line cites Hickman et al. (2021), and the graphic is branded by Our World in Data.

The six statements cover several dimensions of climate concern: existential fear (“Humanity is doomed”), fear about personal or family stability (“Family security is threatened”), intergenerational expectations (“Less opportunity than their parents”), reproductive hesitation (“Hesitant to have children”), generalized fear (“Future is frightening”), and perceived collective failure (“People have failed to take care of the planet”).

The “All countries” values are 56% for “Humanity is doomed,” 52% for “Family security is threatened,” 55% for “Less opportunity than their parents,” 39% for “Hesitant to have children,” 75% for “Future is frightening,” and 83% for “People have failed to take care of the planet.”
There is substantial variation by country within the same statement.
For “Humanity is doomed,” values range from 42% in Nigeria to 74% in India.
For “Family security is threatened,” they range from 30% in Finland to 77% in the Philippines.
For “Less opportunity than their parents,” they range from 42% in Finland to 70% in the Philippines.
For “Hesitant to have children,” they range from 23% in Nigeria to 48% in Brazil.
For “Future is frightening,” they range from 56% in Finland to 92% in the Philippines.
For “People have failed to take care of the planet,” they range from 75% in Finland to 93% in the Philippines.
derived_claims: The purpose appears to be comparing levels of climate anxiety or climate concern across countries and across different types of worries. — derived from the six survey statements and country comparisons

Across the chart, the highest percentages tend to appear for “People have failed to take care of the planet” and “Future is frightening,” indicating that broad moral judgment and fear about the future are more widely endorsed than the most extreme statement, “Humanity is doomed.” — derived by comparing the labeled percentages across the six panels
This suggests concern is widespread, but not all forms of concern are equally intense or equally personal. — derived by contrasting all-country percentages across statement types

The chart shows that majorities in the all-country summary agree with five of the six statements, and nearly two in five agree they are hesitant to have children. — derived by reading the all-country values and counting statements above 50%

For example, the Philippines is at or near the top on several statements, including 92% for “Future is frightening” and 93% for “People have failed to take care of the planet,” while some countries such as Finland and the United States are lower on several measures. — derived by comparing labeled country values across panels
The Philippines appears among the highest responses in multiple categories, while Finland appears among the lowest in several categories. — derived by comparing country ranks across panels
speculative_claims: In climate psychology and public-opinion research, differences like these can indicate that moral concern and anticipatory anxiety are more common than concrete life-course changes such as deciding not to have children. — source: climate psychology/public opinion research
Young people are a directly affected group because they are likely to live through more of the long-term consequences of climate change than older generations. — source: climate impacts/demography

If these attitudes are widespread, they may matter for mental health services, education, family planning conversations, and climate communication strategies aimed at youth. — source: public health/education policy
